prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: システム連携用語表 (language ja).
Grid: 3 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "用語" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 210px
  col 2: header "英語" · longest unbreakable word 103px · one-line width 163px
  col 3: header "説明" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 860px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"col 1 is squeezed to a single character per line, so every term becomes a vertical stack of 6–11 glyphs (イ/ン/タ/ー/ポ…). The row headers — the thing a glossary is scanned by — stop reading as words. col 2 and col 3 are generous, but the scan column is sacrificed to buy that."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"A sensible balance: col 1 holds about five characters per line so terms stay recognisable in 2–3 lines, col 2 is wide enough that 'interoperability' and 'transaction manager' keep their word shapes, and col 3 gets the widest measure of the three-column split (~8 characters per line, six lines per definition). Minor cost: compounds like トランザクション|マネージャー break mid-term."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"col 2 is pulled in just past the breaking point, so 'interoperability' splits into 'interoperabilit' + a dangling 'y' — a visible defect on the key English term. col 1 gains a little room and col 3 stays at ~6 characters per line, so rows are tall; nothing is broken beyond that, but D achieves the same proportions without the split word."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"col 1 is the roomiest of the narrow-header options (~7 characters), so loanword compounds split closer to their natural joints (トランザクション|マネージャ), and col 2 still keeps every English term whole. The price is a tighter 説明 column (~6 characters per line), which makes rows taller and the prose more ragged than B/F."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"col 1 at ~5 characters and col 2 keeping English words intact, while 説明 gets a slightly wider measure than D (~7 characters per line). Middle-of-the-road compromise: nothing broken, nothing excellent — col 1 still breaks マネージャー across lines."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Effectively the same trade as B: readable multi-character row headers, English terms held whole in col 2, and the widest 説明 measure (~8 characters per line, six lines per definition) so the long prose column drives row height least.
